screens.title: Setting Up Your C Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll prepare a reliable workspace for C programming so you can write fast, low-level code with confidence. We'll install and verify GCC on Linux, Mac O S, and Windows, set up Visual Studio Code with the recommended C/C++ extensions, and run your first compiled program. You will also learn the four compilation stages — preprocessing, compilation to assembly, assembly to object code, and linking — so you can interpret compiler messages and fix errors. This matters because C gives you direct control over memory and performance; without a correct toolchain and editor setup, small mistakes like a missing PATH entry or an unsaved file will stop you from running code and slow your learning. By the end you'll be able to compile a simple program from the terminal, debug a common syntax error, and know where to look when the system reports "command not found". To get started, follow the OS-specific install steps we present, then create and compile a Hello, World! source file to confirm everything works.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll build concrete skills that let you run C programs locally. First, you'll install a working C compiler, typically GCC, on whichever operating system you use. This means running the right package command on Linux, installing command line tools on Mac O S, or installing MinGW-w64 on Windows and adding its bin directory to PATH. Second, you'll set up Visual Studio Code with the recommended C/C++ extension pack, enabling code completion and debugging support so editing and fixing errors is faster. Third, you'll write, compile, and run a Hello, World! program. This simple program proves the toolchain is functional and introduces the compile-and-run commands that you'll use repeatedly. Fourth, you'll learn the four compilation stages—preprocessing, compilation to assembly, assembly to object code, and linking—so that when the compiler reports an error you know which stage produced it and where to look next. These objectives move you from an empty machine to a functional development workflow and reduce friction so you can focus on learning C itself.

screens.title: Installing GCC on Linux, macOS, and Windows
screens.narratorSegment: Installing GCC varies by operating system, but the goal is the same: have a working gcc command in your terminal. On most Linux distributions, the simplest path is to install the build-essential package. That bundle includes GCC and essential tools. Open your terminal, update packages, and install build-essential; after installation run a version check to confirm. On Mac O S the recommended approach is to install the Xcode Command Line Tools. This provides a GCC-compatible toolchain accessible from the terminal after you run the installer command and follow the prompts. On Windows, a native port of GCC is provided by MinGW-w64 or MSYS2. Install MinGW-w64 with its installer, choose an appropriate architecture, and then make sure to add the MinGW bin folder to your PATH environment variable so typing gcc from any command prompt works. A common misconception is expecting a graphical installer to automatically add PATH entries; on Windows you may need to edit environment variables yourself. After any install, verify with the simple command to display the compiler version. That check confirms both the installation and the PATH configuration.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Installing GCC
Installation Steps
Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
Open terminal and run: sudo apt update && sudo apt install build-essential
macOS
Run: xcode-select --install to install the Command Line Tools which include GCC.
Windows (MinGW-w64)
Install MinGW-w64, then add the MinGW bin folder to PATH so gcc is available.
Verification
Check compiler
Run gcc --version in a new terminal window and confirm version output appears.
Common Pitfalls & Fixes
  • For Windows, forgetting to add MinGW's bin to PATH leads to "command not found"; update environment variables and restart the shell.
  • On macOS, if the installer fails, confirm you have administrative permissions and an updated OS version.
  • On Linux, ensure you ran the package update command before installing build-essential so dependencies are current.
Pro Tip

Open a fresh terminal after changing PATH so environment changes take effect. Old shells keep the previous PATH.

screens.title: Your First C Program: Hello, World!
screens.narratorSegment: Writing and running a Hello, World! program verifies the full toolchain and introduces the compile-and-run workflow you'll use constantly. Create a new file named hello. c and include the standard input/output header at the top. Define the main function, call the print function to display text, and return zero for successful execution. Save the file. Then open a terminal in the same folder and run the compile command: instruct gcc to build the source and write an executable name. After the compiler finishes without errors, run the executable from the shell and you will see your message printed. A common misconception is that the editor runs the program; in compiled languages like C you must explicitly compile to create an executable before running it. Also remember to save the file before compiling — unsaved edits won't be included. This step teaches the essential loop: edit, save, compile, run, and read compiler messages to fix any syntax errors you introduced. Your First C Program: Hello, World! means saving before compiling and naming the executable clearly will avoid confusion and confirm your setup works.. In practical terms, create hello.c, compile with gcc, and run the executable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Hello, World!
Source File
#include <stdio.h> // Include the standard input/output library

int main() { // The main function, where program execution begins
    printf("Hello, World!
"); // Print the message to the console
    return 0; // Indicate successful program execution
}
Save as hello.c. Then compile with gcc hello.c -o hello and run with ./hello (Windows: hello.exe).
What to watch for
  • Missing semicolons produce syntax errors; read the reported line number and check surrounding lines.
  • Unsaved changes: the compiler reads the saved file on disk, not your unsaved editor buffer.
  • Using the wrong working directory means gcc won't find your source file; use the terminal's pwd or cd commands to confirm location.
Key Takeaway

The compile step produces an executable that you must run; saving the file and checking the working directory avoids most early headaches.

screens.title: Key Terms: Source Code, Object Code, Executable, Compiler
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding terminology helps you interpret errors and the files created during build steps. Source code is the human-readable C you write and save with a. c extension. Object code is machine code produced by the assembler from assembly output; it typically lives in files with an. o extension and may contain unresolved references. The executable is the final linked program that the operating system can run directly. The compiler is the tool that translates source code into assembly and prepares it for assembly into object code. A subtle but important difference is between the compiler and the linker: the compiler handles syntax and translation, while the linker resolves references to library functions and produces the executable. Misconceptions include thinking object files are runnable—they’re not until linked—and assuming the linker only matters for large programs; even small programs need linking for standard functions like the print function to work. Recognizing these terms lets you map messages like "undefined reference" to the linking stage and "syntax error" to the compilation stage. Key Terms: Source Code, Object Code, Executable, Compiler means mapping error messages to the appropriate build stage makes debugging faster: syntax errors → compiler, undefined references → linker.. In practical terms, clear definitions you will use when reading compiler messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Key Terms
Source Code
Human-readable C code saved as .c. This is the starting point you edit.
Example: hello.c
Object Code
Produced by the assembler, contains machine instructions but may have unresolved references. Usually .o.
Not directly runnable until linked.
Executable
Final linked program the OS can run. On Unix-like systems it may be named without an extension; on Windows it uses .exe.
Compiler vs Linker
The compiler translates source to assembly and flags syntax errors. The linker combines object files and libraries to resolve references. If you see "undefined reference" the problem is in linking, not syntax.

screens.title: The Four Stages of Compilation
screens.narratorSegment: When you run the single gcc command, several distinct stages take place. First, the preprocessor handles directives that begin with a hash sign. It expands included headers and macros, producing an expanded source file. This stage is why header contents appear available to your code even though you only wrote the include line. Second, the compiler proper translates that expanded source into assembly code — a human-readable low-level form. Third, the assembler converts the assembly into machine code stored in an object file. That object file contains compiled code but may reference external symbols like library functions. Fourth, the linker combines one or more object files with library code to create the final executable; it resolves external references so the program can run. Understanding these stages helps you know where errors are generated: syntax and type issues arise during compilation, while missing libraries or unresolved symbols appear at link time. This mapping makes error messages actionable and reduces time spent guessing where to look. The Four Stages of Compilation means identify whether a problem comes from preprocessing, compilation, assembly, or linking to target your fix quickly.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Compilation Stages
Stages Overview
  1. Preprocessing — expands #include and macros into an expanded source.
  2. Compilation — translates preprocessed code into assembly language.
  3. Assembly — converts assembly into machine code object files.
  4. Linking — combines object files and libraries into a runnable executable.
Inputs and Outputs
Input: hello.c
After preprocessing: expanded source (internal)
After compilation: assembly file (e.g., hello.s)
After assembly: object file (hello.o)
After linking: executable (hello or hello.exe)
Misconception

Seeing a syntax error does not mean linking failed. Syntax errors are handled earlier, during compilation, so fix code structure first.

screens.title: Editor vs IDE: Text Editor with Terminal or VS Code
screens.narratorSegment: You can write C in any plain text editor and compile from the terminal, but using an integrated development environment like Visual Studio Code speeds common tasks and reduces friction. A plain editor is lightweight and familiar, but it offers minimal feedback beyond basic syntax coloring. V S Code with the C/C++ Extension Pack adds intelligent code completion, signature help, and debugging integration. This helps you spot mistakes earlier and step through code when needed. The integrated terminal keeps your workflow in one window so you can edit, save, compile, and run without switching applications. A common misconception is that IDEs hide how compilation works; in reality, V S Code surfaces compiler messages in the terminal and lets you control compile commands directly. For beginners, the combination of editor features and the terminal is the most productive: you still use the same gcc commands, but with better editor feedback and optional debug breakpoints as you advance. Plain Editor + Terminal
  • Very lightweight, minimal configuration.
  • Use your preferred editor and run gcc in a separate terminal.
  • Less help for finding mistakes before compiling.
VS Code + C/C++ Extension

screens.title: PATH and Environment Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Environment variables tell your shell where to find executables. Adding the compiler's bin directory to PATH makes typing gcc available from any folder. Without this, attempting to run gcc produces a "command not found" or equivalent message because the shell doesn't know where to search. On Windows, the common fix is to add the MinGW-w64 bin path to the system PATH via Environment Variables in System Properties. On Mac O S and Linux you can add an export line to your shell profile, but package managers often configure PATH automatically. After editing PATH, open a new terminal window; changes do not affect already-open shells. Always verify by running a simple version check; seeing version information confirms both installation and PATH visibility. A frequent misconception is editing PATH in a single terminal where the change will persist globally; remember to edit persistent environment settings or shell profile files for durable changes. PATH and Environment Variables means always verify path changes in a new terminal and confirm with a version check to avoid false negatives.. In practical terms, why adding the compiler to path matters and how to test it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › PATH & Environment
How PATH Works
The PATH variable lists directories the shell searches for executables. When you type gcc, the shell looks through each PATH entry to find the program. If it can't find it, you'll see a "command not found" message.
Verify
Run gcc --version. If you see version text, PATH is correct.
Fixing on Windows
  1. Locate the MinGW-w64 installation and find the bin folder.
  2. Open System Properties → Environment Variables → Path and add a new entry pointing to that bin folder.
  3. Close and reopen your terminal to apply the change and run gcc --version.
Remember: edits to PATH require a new shell session to take effect.

screens.title: Common Setup and Compile Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Early errors often share simple causes and straightforward fixes. If the shell reports that gcc is not recognized, the usual issue is that the compiler binary is not in PATH. Install the compiler correctly and add the bin directory to PATH, then restart your terminal. Syntax errors from the compiler almost always mean a typo such as a missing semicolon, misspelled function, or unmatched brace; the compiler message will point to a line to inspect. Linking errors like undefined reference occur when the linker cannot find a symbol, which may happen if you forgot to include a library or if you compiled but forgot to link required object files. Another frequent mistake is compiling the wrong file name or not saving recent edits; confirm the working directory and save before building. When debugging, reproduce the error, read the exact compiler output, and resolve the problem closest to the reported stage — syntax fixes before worrying about linking issues. These steps reduce guesswork and teach you to use compiler diagnostics as a guide. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Troubleshooting
"gcc' not recognized"
Cause: compiler binary not found on PATH. Fix: add the compiler's bin folder to PATH, restart the shell, and verify with gcc --version.
Common compilation errors
  • Missing semicolon — syntax error; check the reported line and the line before it.
  • Misspelled identifier — fix the name to match definition.
  • Unmatched braces or parentheses — ensure all open tokens are closed.
Linker errors
Cause: unresolved external symbols typically because code references library functions without linking the appropriate libraries or missing object files. Fix by adding required object files or link flags, and ensure functions are defined.
Quick checklist
  1. Save the file before compiling.
  2. Confirm you are in the correct directory.
  3. Read the exact compiler message and fix the closest reported issue.
Common Mistake

Don't guess fixes. Use the compiler's stage hint: syntax issues require code changes, linker issues require adding libraries or object files, and PATH issues require environment changes.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll prepare a reliable workspace for C programming so you can write fast, low-level code with confidence. We'll install and verify GCC on Linux, Mac O S, and Windows, set up Visual Studio Code with the recommended C/C++ extensions, and run your first compiled program. You will also learn the four compilation stages — preprocessing, compilation to assembly, assembly to object code, and linking — so you can interpret compiler messages and fix errors. This matters because C gives you direct control over memory and performance; without a correct toolchain and editor setup, small mistakes like a missing PATH entry or an unsaved file will stop you from running code and slow your learning. By the end you'll be able to compile a simple program from the terminal, debug a common syntax error, and know where to look when the system reports "command not found". To get started, follow the OS-specific install steps we present, then create and compile a Hello, World! source file to confirm everything works.

Over the next screens you'll build concrete skills that let you run C programs locally. First, you'll install a working C compiler, typically GCC, on whichever operating system you use. This means running the right package command on Linux, installing command line tools on Mac O S, or installing MinGW-w64 on Windows and adding its bin directory to PATH. Second, you'll set up Visual Studio Code with the recommended C/C++ extension pack, enabling code completion and debugging support so editing and fixing errors is faster. Third, you'll write, compile, and run a Hello, World! program. This simple program proves the toolchain is functional and introduces the compile-and-run commands that you'll use repeatedly. Fourth, you'll learn the four compilation stages—preprocessing, compilation to assembly, assembly to object code, and linking—so that when the compiler reports an error you know which stage produced it and where to look next. These objectives move you from an empty machine to a functional development workflow and reduce friction so you can focus on learning C itself.

These additional objectives focus on verification and troubleshooting so your environment keeps working as you code. You will learn to check that gcc is installed by running a simple version check and to confirm your IDE is configured by opening an integrated terminal and compiling a small file. You will practice adding MinGW's bin directory to the PATH on Windows so the system can locate the gcc command. You'll also complete a guided hands-on task: create a personalized greeting program, save it with a. c extension, compile it with gcc, and execute the result. This hands-on loop teaches habits that prevent common mistakes, like compiling an unsaved file or using the wrong working directory. Finally, you'll be able to interpret common compiler messages such as syntax errors for missing semicolons or undefined references during linking. Learning to read these messages early makes debugging faster and reduces frustration as programs grow more complex.

Installing GCC varies by operating system, but the goal is the same: have a working gcc command in your terminal. On most Linux distributions, the simplest path is to install the build-essential package. That bundle includes GCC and essential tools. Open your terminal, update packages, and install build-essential; after installation run a version check to confirm. On Mac O S the recommended approach is to install the Xcode Command Line Tools. This provides a GCC-compatible toolchain accessible from the terminal after you run the installer command and follow the prompts. On Windows, a native port of GCC is provided by MinGW-w64 or MSYS2. Install MinGW-w64 with its installer, choose an appropriate architecture, and then make sure to add the MinGW bin folder to your PATH environment variable so typing gcc from any command prompt works. A common misconception is expecting a graphical installer to automatically add PATH entries; on Windows you may need to edit environment variables yourself. After any install, verify with the simple command to display the compiler version. That check confirms both the installation and the PATH configuration.

Writing and running a Hello, World! program verifies the full toolchain and introduces the compile-and-run workflow you'll use constantly. Create a new file named hello. c and include the standard input/output header at the top. Define the main function, call the print function to display text, and return zero for successful execution. Save the file. Then open a terminal in the same folder and run the compile command: instruct gcc to build the source and write an executable name. After the compiler finishes without errors, run the executable from the shell and you will see your message printed. A common misconception is that the editor runs the program; in compiled languages like C you must explicitly compile to create an executable before running it. Also remember to save the file before compiling — unsaved edits won't be included. This step teaches the essential loop: edit, save, compile, run, and read compiler messages to fix any syntax errors you introduced. Understanding terminology helps you interpret errors and the files created during build steps. Source code is the human-readable C you write and save with a. c extension. Object code is machine code produced by the assembler from assembly output; it typically lives in files with an. o extension and may contain unresolved references. The executable is the final linked program that the operating system can run directly. The compiler is the tool that translates source code into assembly and prepares it for assembly into object code. A subtle but important difference is between the compiler and the linker: the compiler handles syntax and translation, while the linker resolves references to library functions and produces the executable. Misconceptions include thinking object files are runnable—they’re not until linked—and assuming the linker only matters for large programs; even small programs need linking for standard functions like the print function to work. Recognizing these terms lets you map messages like "undefined reference" to the linking stage and "syntax error" to the compilation stage. When you run the single gcc command, several distinct stages take place. First, the preprocessor handles directives that begin with a hash sign. It expands included headers and macros, producing an expanded source file. This stage is why header contents appear available to your code even though you only wrote the include line. Second, the compiler proper translates that expanded source into assembly code — a human-readable low-level form. Third, the assembler converts the assembly into machine code stored in an object file. That object file contains compiled code but may reference external symbols like library functions. Fourth, the linker combines one or more object files with library code to create the final executable; it resolves external references so the program can run. Understanding these stages helps you know where errors are generated: syntax and type issues arise during compilation, while missing libraries or unresolved symbols appear at link time. This mapping makes error messages actionable and reduces time spent guessing where to look.
